english.html: approached in these two countries; and at each fact he particularly designates certain persons with whom inquiry can be made (as has since been done, and the whole verified), to render what he said still more persuasive and probable.

These matters here discoursed at length, and the multitude of so many and so many tokens so true, gave the Judges great occasion to persuade themselves of the innocence of the said du Tilh, and moreover to wonder at the happiness and felicity of his memory, which had known how to recite innumerable things done and past more than twenty years ago; wherein the commissioners, who by all means possible to them strove to catch him in some lie, could nevertheless gain nothing upon him, nor prevent him from answering truly to all things, on which nevertheless he was by them separately and at intervals interrogated. Which drew the judges more and more into wonder, who, for the great felicity of so happy a memory, would gladly have compared him to a Scipio, Cyrus, Theodectes, Mithridates, Themistocles, Cineas, Metrodorus or Lucullus, persons excellent in the gift of memory, and eternally celebrated <sup class="mk" data-key="a">a</sup>, if the wretched end of this prodigious cheat had not offended the splendour of such and so well-marked persons, by comparing to them so impudent, deplorable and wretched a man <sup class="mk" data-key="b">b</sup>. Certainly, if one could without scruple make use of such comparisons, it would be very apt with Porcius Latro, the great companion of Seneca, who boasted that he had never been deceived by his memory in a single word; and, to make trial of it, would often have proposed to him the name of some ancient captain or other illustrious and renowned person, at the pleasure of him who named him, of whom on the spot he would recite from top to bottom the pure truth of all the deeds since his

notes.original: Ciceron au i. des Tuſcula. nes, & au ſecond de Oratore. Pline au liure vij. cha. xxiiij.
notes.gloss: The stock roll of prodigious memories: Cyrus, who knew every soldier by name; L. Scipio, the Roman people; Cineas, the senate the day after his arrival; Mithridates, the twenty-two languages of his subjects; Metrodorus; Theodectes; Themistocles; Lucullus's memory is Cicero's, Academica II.1–2.

notes.citation: Coras, Annotation XII (cross-reference, as printed; the bearing is not evident — Annotation XII treats change of name and substitution of persons — and the print's numbering of headings is unreliable, Annotation XVIII being printed XIII)
